Surviving Photographs of Self Winding Clock Co. / Western Union “Naval Observatory Time” Clocks: An Illustrated Catalogue

A working catalogue compiled from public photographic archives.

Educational edition — a non-commercial research resource. Revised 19 September 2026.

The Self Winding Clock Company of New York (1886–c. 1969) manufactured battery-wound clocks that were corrected once an hour by an electrical pulse carried over Western Union’s telegraph lines and referred to the master clock of the U.S. Naval Observatory; their dials read “Naval Observatory Time — Western Union.” Although roughly 100,000 were in service by 1940, the firm is sparsely documented online. This catalogue assembles photographs in which such a clock is identifiable.

1. Scope and method

Entries were located in freely accessible digital collections and verified by inspection of the image itself. Two grades of identification are used. Dial confirmed denotes a photograph in which the “Naval Observatory Time / Western Union” wording, or the Self Winding Clock Co. imprint, is legible. In situ denotes a clock visible on the wall of a documented Western Union workplace where the make cannot be read directly; because Western Union offices were equipped from this system, such clocks are very likely of the same manufacture, but the attribution is not certified here.

4. The source of the signal

5. How the national time network worked

The clocks in this catalogue were the visible end of a chain that reached from an astronomer’s telescope to a wall in a country depot. At the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington, true time was determined from the stars and held by three precision pendulum clocks — the reference standard, not the Self Winding Clock Co. product — sealed in an underground vault.

Each day at 11:50 a.m. Eastern, Western Union handed its wires to the government. A “sending” clock, checked against the vault standards to a fraction of a second, was looped through transcontinental lines to San Diego, Key West, Arlington and Annapolis; at the stroke of 11:55 it “threw a single switch: ‘Click!’ and standard time was going out to all the world.” The noon signal ran five minutes, with a ten-second silence just before the stroke of noon, and was sent three times a day — noon, 10 p.m. and 3 a.m. Eastern (World’s Work, 1930).

Locally, a Western Union office kept a master clock, set right at noon by that signal, which then corrected every subscriber clock in the town once an hour — which is why the dials read “Naval Observatory Time, hourly by Western Union.” By 1930 the article counted “more than 150,000 subscribers.” A business paid roughly $15 to $30 a year, “including installation, complete maintenance, and the time service” (Milham, Time and Timekeepers, 1923).

6. How the clocks were installed and wired

A self-winding clock needed no power cord: two dry cells inside the case drove a small motor that rewound the mainspring once an hour. The only outside connection was a thin, low-voltage synchronizing wire that entered the back of the case and ran into the wall, with the case mounted flush — which is why these clocks look wireless in nearly every photograph.

A whole building was run as a system: one master clock, usually in a back room, drove the subscriber and “secondary” dials — and program circuits that rang bells on a schedule — over low-voltage wiring threaded from room to room. The public saw a wall of clocks that looked wireless; the wiring converged out of sight at the master.

7. A note: the clock that timed an execution

A measure of how completely these clocks stood for “the correct time”: at the execution of Bruno Hauptmann (the Lindbergh case) at the New Jersey State Prison in April 1936, the death chamber’s official clock was a Western Union / Naval Observatory Time clock. The Brooklyn Daily Eagle’s account records the officials checking it in the moment — “It is 8:35. There is argument about the time — is the clock two minutes fast?” — the dial reading, as always, “Naval Observatory Time, hourly by Western Union.”
